newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Antarctic ozone hole may set new record.
newsitem.headline: Antarctic ozone hole may set new record.

text.p: The hole in the ozone layer which forms annually over the Antarctic during the Southern Hemisphere spring is already twice the size of Europe, a U.N. agency said on Friday.
The World Meteorological Organisation said the hole had appeared earlier than in recent years, but it would only know next week whether the depletion level exceeds the 1995 record.

The hole in the earth's protective layer now covers more than 20 million square km (7.7 million square miles), "twice the surface of Europe from the Atlantic to the Ural mountains," the Geneva-based agency said in a statement.
The previous record over the Antarctic was 22 million square kms (8.5 million square miles), set last year.

"Every year we find a relatively large hole. We may end up with a larger hole than last year, but it is not yet certain. It will depend partly on the atmosphere circulating in the stratosphere," WMO's Frederic Delsol told Reuters.
"The situation so far conforms with what was expected. We will know better by the middle of next week," he added.

The ozone, a fragile shield of gas which absorbs and blocks most ultra-violet rays of the Sun, is being depleted by man-made chemicals. These include chloroflurocarbons (used in aerosols and refrigeration), the pesticide methyl bromide and solvents.
Any sustained surge in radiation reaching the Earth could lead to a rise in cancer in humans and animals, lower crop yields and affect the marine food chain, according to experts.
WMO blamed the latest destruction on "continuous increase in the concentrations of chlorine loading in the stratosphere".

Reporting data from WMO satellite and observing stations in the zone between September 24-30, WMO said an elliptical, elongated hole in the ozone over the Antarctic had occured somewhat earlier than in the previous few years.

"The surface covered by the ozone hole has well exceeded 20 million square kilometres and ozone values of less than 180 units (deficiency greater than 45 per cent) cover nearly the entire continent," WMO's Dr. Rumen Bojkov was quoted as saying.
Scientists concur that an ozone hole exists when values are less than 200 units.
For the third consecutive week, the ozone in the lower stratosphere, at altitudes of between 17 to 22 km (10 to 14 miles) over the Antarctic was "nearly completely annihilated".
"It seems apparent that the past month has disclosed new low ozone values which are within the same magnitude of the extremes noted during the last three-four Antarctic spring seasons.

"Consequently we are observing confirmation that with the continuous increase in the concentrations of chlorine loading in the stratosphere the ozone destruction is becoming worse, providing favourable circulation patterns exist and especially when the stratospheric temperatures are very low," it added.
Cold is a major factor facilitating ozone destruction by man-made compounds containing chlorine and bromine.
Under the 1987 Montreal Protocol of the Vienna Convention, governments agreed to phase out chemicals destroying the ozone.
Industrialised countries have banned chlorofluorocarbons, halons and carbon tetrachloride, while developing countries have until the year 2010 to conform.

Industrialised countries will phase out hydrochlorofluorocarbons by the year 2030 and were to freeze methyl bromide levels by last year. Developing countries have not yet agreed to control measures for these two substances.
WMO, in a statement issued last March, said such measures would assist the process of healing the damage to the ozone.
"However, not until the second half of the 21st Century could one expect the disappearance of the Antarctic-spring ozone hole phenomena," the agency said at the time.
